statement: The figures in this claim are second-hand: they come from one narrative review of the survey literature, not from studies the editors have read in full, and the review itself reports that no laboratory study has ever given humans a series of MDMA doses, so chronic tolerance cannot be studied in people under blind, placebo-controlled conditions. In that review, most people who use ecstasy regularly say its wanted effects decline with repeated use: 58% of 1151 readers of a dance magazine reported tolerance, and about 85-95% of 430 people using it regularly reported a decline in subjective efficacy, with the first occasion often described as the strongest. Reported doses rise with past use: from 1.2 to 1.8 tablets a session in the same 430 people, from 100% of 109 people in a novice group reporting a usual dose of 1-2 tablets to 62% of 37 in the heaviest group, and from 0% to 35% reporting a maximum of ten or more tablets in a week. One study ran the other way, with the longer-using group taking slightly fewer tablets per occasion. All of this is self-reported by people taking tablets of unknown content, compared across groups rather than followed over time, with about half the comparisons coming from the reviewer's own research group; the same surveys also report more problems attributed to ecstasy in the heavier-using groups, so nothing here separates tolerance from the other reasons people take more (Parrott, 2005).
plain: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well, and the first time is often described as the best. Across surveys, people who have used it more say they take more tablets. But these are answers on questionnaires, from people taking tablets whose contents nobody checked, comparing different groups of people rather than following the same people over time, so we cannot tell how much of this is the drug and how much is everything else. No laboratory has ever given people repeated doses over weeks, so there is no controlled study of this at all.
population: People who use ecstasy recreationally, in surveys and interview studies from Australia, the United Kingdom, the United States and continental Europe, in samples of 52 to about 1151 people, as summarized in one narrative review
exposure: Repeated recreational use of tablets sold as ecstasy, over months to years, in amounts self-reported as tablets per occasion and lifetime occasions; the MDMA content of the tablets was not measured in any of the studies summarized
comparator: Groups of people with less past use in the same surveys, and each person's own account of their earlier use
outcome: Self-reported decline in the wanted effects, self-reported tablets per occasion and maximum tablets, and self-attributed problems
magnitude: Self-reported tolerance: 58% of 1151 people; about 85-95% of 430 people using ecstasy regularly; 67% of those with six or more occasions in an earlier survey said positive effects decreased and negative effects increased. Dose: 1.8 tablets a session currently against 1.2 when starting (430 people); usual dose 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets and maximum ever 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7) across groups of 14, 14 and 11 people defined by lifetime use (maximum p<0.01; usual dose only p<0.10); a usual dose of 1-2 tablets reported by 100%, 84% and 62% of groups of 109, 136 and 37 people, and a maximum of ten or more tablets in a week by 0%, 9% and 35% (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, p<0.001). Against this, two groups differing in duration of use (3.9 against 10.9 years) and lifetime consumption (223 against 811 tablets) reported 2.5 against 2.1 tablets per occasion, not significantly different.

evidence.locator: The paragraph beginning 'The pharmacodynamic effects of single doses of MDMA' and the one following it (left column); Subjective reports of tolerance and diminishing responsiveness to MDMA, 2nd-3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review states that no laboratory study has given a series of MDMA doses to humans and that chronic tolerance therefore cannot be investigated in humans under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions, so all human evidence comes from surveys of people who use ecstasy recreationally; in those surveys 58% of 1151 people reported tolerance and about 85-95% of 430 people using it regularly reported declining subjective efficacy, with an earlier survey finding 67% of those with six or more occasions reporting that positive effects decreased and negative effects increased.

evidence.locator: Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Table 1; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Reported dose rises with past use: 1.8 tablets a session currently against 1.2 when starting in 430 people; usual dose 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets and maximum ever 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7) across lifetime-use groups of 14, 14 and 11 people, with the maximum significant at p<0.01 and the usual dose only at p<0.10; and a usual dose of 1-2 tablets reported by 100% of 109, 84% of 136 and 62% of 37 people in novice, moderate and heaviest groups, with a maximum of ten or more tablets in a week reported by 0%, 9% and 35% (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, p<0.001).

evidence.locator: The paragraph beginning 'A related problem is the issue of dosage' (p. 72); Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, last paragraph (p. 75); Table 3 (p. 78)
evidence.extracted: Qualifications reported in the same review: one study found no dose escalation with longer use (2.1 tablets per occasion after 10.9 years against 2.5 after 3.9 years, not significant); average MDMA content per tablet in United Kingdom forensic samples fell about 20% across the mid-1990s (102 to 88 mg, then 75 to 73 mg) so falling tablet strength cannot be excluded for studies from that period; and in the same internet sample, problems attributed to ecstasy rose with lifetime use (depression 33%, 54% and 65%; memory problems 19%, 52% and 73%), so heavier use goes with more reported harm as well as with larger doses.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional self-report of illegal drug use with no biological verification and no measurement of what the tablets contained, seen only through a narrative review with no search strategy, no selection criteria and no appraisal of the studies it cites, about half of them by the reviewer's own group.

inconsistency.note: Most surveys point the same way; the one study that does not is reported in the claim.

indirectness.note: The editors have not read the primary studies: every figure is second-hand from the review (METHODS 6.3). Self-reported tolerance is also an indirect measure of a pharmacological change.

imprecision.note: The samples are large by the standards of this literature (hundreds to over a thousand); imprecision is not what limits this claim.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low. Risk of bias -2 for unverified self-report of unknown substances in unsystematically selected studies; indirectness -1 because the figures are second-hand from a narrative review and self-reported tolerance is an indirect measure. Certainty very-low. No upgrade for a dose-response gradient: the gradient here is between groups of different people, not within people over time, and the same gradient appears in self-attributed harms, which suggests shared reporting influences. The claim stays at draft and says in its first sentence that its figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3).

verification.flag_note: Rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and is not shown in the at-a-glance box (METHODS 6.3). If the senior author wants this question on the page at a higher rung, the primary surveys (Verheyden et al., 2003a; Winstock et al., 2001; Scholey et al., 2004; Fox et al., 2001a and 2001b; Verkes et al., 2001; Topp et al., 1999) need to be read in full.

changelog.change: New draft claim from Parrott (2005), read in full (card sc_parrott_2005). Section 5 asks about tolerance on every page; this is the only evidence there is about tolerance to MDMA over months and years, and it is survey evidence seen through one narrative review, so the claim is worded to say that and stays at draft.
